compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In the fictional release incident, both people can pay attention to what is happening and ask for observable facts. That illustrates the shared E and S preferences. Response time and tone may reflect who is on duty or what information they have.

The difference sits in the other two places. Which basis judgement cites more often: "can this standard be applied to every channel consistently", or "what does this step mean for people who have already paid". And which stance the outward arrangement takes: settle the wording and the order now, or hold until the next round of metrics. Both are available at once; the difference is which one is used first to persuade.

### The same rollback call: two trade-offs, not two speeds

Align the conditions first: the same dashboard, the same change ticket, the same handling authority, the same forty minutes left. Either can check the dashboard, notify support, or follow the runbook. What is comparable is not who moves first, but which kind of basis each more often uses to support a position while information is still incomplete.

One trade-off starts from the people: will this action make people who have already been charged pay twice, what can support say publicly right now, and how do we correct a statement issued too early. On the outward side, it more often wants to fix now who notifies whom and when to reassess, so the people waiting in the group have a definite answer. The cost is that the public line may be set before the facts, and the second statement becomes harder to write.

The other trade-off starts from measurable quantity: how many points the success rate has dropped, which data centre the failures concentrate in, and whether that criterion can be applied consistently across all channels. On the outward side, it more often prefers not to fix anything yet, closing once the next round of metrics arrives, so nothing has to be retracted immediately. The cost is that complaints may pile up while people wait, and support has nothing it can say.

Keep the counterexamples in both directions. Someone starting from the people will also demand that an entry point be closed at once, having calculated that it will not affect anyone mid-payment; someone starting from quantity will also ask support to send a short holding line because the channels are already pressing. Neither changes the direction of the preference; both show the two approaches are within range.

Sequence is not a criterion. Whoever has years of on-call experience, of either type, is more likely to walk the runbook once first; who holds the change authority that day and who is the shift lead often override preference. The same person may take the other approach on another shift.

### Why Fe and Ti are shared but sit in different places

The common four-function notation used here puts ESFJ at Fe–Si–Ne–Ti and ESTP at Se–Ti–Fe–Ni. Two names overlap: Fe and Ti. What changes is the perceiving side: Si and Ne against Se and Ni.

The two shared processes do not sit in the same place: Fe is dominant in ESFJ and third in ESTP; Ti is inferior in ESFJ and auxiliary in ESTP. A different position only means this writing places them in different slots; it does not explain when they appear, how practised they are, or who is better at anything.

The four preference letters each cover one thing. T/F covers what goes on the scales when choosing: a standard that can be applied consistently, or what the people involved have to carry. J/P covers the outward step: tightening the arrangement, or loosening it and waiting. The two cannot substitute for each other, and neither can be measured by how fast someone talks or how soft the tone is.

The third position is not the same process on both sides: Ne is third for ESFJ, Fe is third for ESTP, and Ni is fourth for ESTP. Whether that slot carries an attitude label is handled differently across tables; this page lists the common writing and does not present it as the only version. The disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain who speaks first. The preferences are set out one by one in the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the scenes below are fictional and are used only to compare ways of communicating and organising information; they correspond to no real person or event. Whether and when to roll back follows your own service runbook and authority — this page provides no handling procedure; where money and customer data are involved, follow internal process and professional guidance first.

When the two work together, the usual sticking point is messages falling out of sync in the group: one is waiting for a number that can be stated publicly, the other is waiting for a scope that can be confirmed internally. It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of basis each needs first.

### Forty minutes after release: payment success rate falling

(Fictional scene.) Forty minutes after a new version ships, the payment success rate is below normal and complaints are coming in. Both hold the same dashboard, the same change ticket and the same permissions.

One handling pulls the affected list, groups it by channel, gives support different wording per channel, and sends the line "we are working on it" to steady the people already waiting. The possible cost is stating an estimated time too early, which makes the second statement harder to write.

The other checks whether failures are concentrated in one part of the service and asks whether the same evidence would justify a change elsewhere. Waiting for firmer evidence can delay an update to support. Either emphasis could inform the same decision, which belongs to the authorised team under its own runbook.

Either can rescue the situation and either can fail. A workable arrangement runs two lines in parallel and agrees a shared checkpoint — for example, at the time set by the incident lead — before deciding on a rollback. The division follows who knows how, who is on shift and who has authority, not type.

The example illustrates how a team can consider customer impact alongside evidence that an action is justified. Real decisions about payments and rollbacks belong to the authorised team and follow its incident procedures.

### The review meeting: how to set the agenda

(Fictional scene.) At the next day's review there are two common agendas. One gives the on-call colleague a few minutes to describe the situation at the time, then walks the timeline item by item. The other aligns the timeline first to establish why the alert came ten minutes late, then comes back to people.

Both have costs. Talking only about the situation may miss the cause of the alert delay once more; walking only the timeline may leave the on-call colleague afraid to hit stop next time. Both have counterexamples: someone arguing to start with the situation will also put the timeline on the whiteboard and go through it, especially when blame has landed on the wrong person; someone arguing to start with the timeline will also ask "who was most tired last night" before getting to the point.

Order is not the criterion; the review is worth something when both happen. When setting the agenda, ask two questions: is what needs changing the process or the communication, and who most needs to be heard in this meeting. Different answers give different agendas, with no relation to type.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Treating "good at caring" as the property of Feeling types is the most common slip in this pair. Caring is a skill built through practice and experience; ESTP may be the first to notice a new colleague's hands shaking and pull them off the desk. Conversely, ESFJ under time pressure may push the schedule and lose track of who was left behind.

Treating "good with numbers" as a marker of Thinking types is equally wrong. ESFJ can work out how many orders a rollback would charge twice, and care more afterwards about how to explain it to customers; ESTP can do the same calculation and want to verify whether the criterion holds first.

The third slip is treating a rollback as a competence issue. "A release should be stable" is an expectation, not evidence about preference; willingness to roll back depends more on whether the criteria were written in advance, how clear the authority is, and whether observation has blind spots.

The fourth deserves its own line: using "called first or opened the dashboard first" as evidence of type. The same action may come from on-call division, change authority, an information gap, or an entirely different reason. Labelling on sight skips the reason, and the difference in this pair lies precisely in the reason.

body: In the fictional release incident, both people can pay attention to what is happening and ask for observable facts. That illustrates the shared E and S preferences. Response time and tone may reflect who is on duty or what information they have.

The difference sits in the other two places. Which basis judgement cites more often: "can this standard be applied to every channel consistently", or "what does this step mean for people who have already paid". And which stance the outward arrangement takes: settle the wording and the order now, or hold until the next round of metrics. Both are available at once; the difference is which one is used first to persuade.
### The same rollback call: two trade-offs, not two speeds

Align the conditions first: the same dashboard, the same change ticket, the same handling authority, the same forty minutes left. Either can check the dashboard, notify support, or follow the runbook. What is comparable is not who moves first, but which kind of basis each more often uses to support a position while information is still incomplete.

One trade-off starts from the people: will this action make people who have already been charged pay twice, what can support say publicly right now, and how do we correct a statement issued too early. On the outward side, it more often wants to fix now who notifies whom and when to reassess, so the people waiting in the group have a definite answer. The cost is that the public line may be set before the facts, and the second statement becomes harder to write.

The other trade-off starts from measurable quantity: how many points the success rate has dropped, which data centre the failures concentrate in, and whether that criterion can be applied consistently across all channels. On the outward side, it more often prefers not to fix anything yet, closing once the next round of metrics arrives, so nothing has to be retracted immediately. The cost is that complaints may pile up while people wait, and support has nothing it can say.

Keep the counterexamples in both directions. Someone starting from the people will also demand that an entry point be closed at once, having calculated that it will not affect anyone mid-payment; someone starting from quantity will also ask support to send a short holding line because the channels are already pressing. Neither changes the direction of the preference; both show the two approaches are within range.

Sequence is not a criterion. Whoever has years of on-call experience, of either type, is more likely to walk the runbook once first; who holds the change authority that day and who is the shift lead often override preference. The same person may take the other approach on another shift.
### Why Fe and Ti are shared but sit in different places
The common four-function notation used here puts ESFJ at Fe–Si–Ne–Ti and ESTP at Se–Ti–Fe–Ni. Two names overlap: Fe and Ti. What changes is the perceiving side: Si and Ne against Se and Ni.

The two shared processes do not sit in the same place: Fe is dominant in ESFJ and third in ESTP; Ti is inferior in ESFJ and auxiliary in ESTP. A different position only means this writing places them in different slots; it does not explain when they appear, how practised they are, or who is better at anything.

The four preference letters each cover one thing. T/F covers what goes on the scales when choosing: a standard that can be applied consistently, or what the people involved have to carry. J/P covers the outward step: tightening the arrangement, or loosening it and waiting. The two cannot substitute for each other, and neither can be measured by how fast someone talks or how soft the tone is.

The third position is not the same process on both sides: Ne is third for ESFJ, Fe is third for ESTP, and Ni is fourth for ESTP. Whether that slot carries an attitude label is handled differently across tables; this page lists the common writing and does not present it as the only version. The disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain who speaks first. The preferences are set out one by one in the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).

body: Scope note: the scenes below are fictional and are used only to compare ways of communicating and organising information; they correspond to no real person or event. Whether and when to roll back follows your own service runbook and authority — this page provides no handling procedure; where money and customer data are involved, follow internal process and professional guidance first.

When the two work together, the usual sticking point is messages falling out of sync in the group: one is waiting for a number that can be stated publicly, the other is waiting for a scope that can be confirmed internally. It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of basis each needs first.
### Forty minutes after release: payment success rate falling

(Fictional scene.) Forty minutes after a new version ships, the payment success rate is below normal and complaints are coming in. Both hold the same dashboard, the same change ticket and the same permissions.

One handling pulls the affected list, groups it by channel, gives support different wording per channel, and sends the line "we are working on it" to steady the people already waiting. The possible cost is stating an estimated time too early, which makes the second statement harder to write.

The other checks whether failures are concentrated in one part of the service and asks whether the same evidence would justify a change elsewhere. Waiting for firmer evidence can delay an update to support. Either emphasis could inform the same decision, which belongs to the authorised team under its own runbook.

Either can rescue the situation and either can fail. A workable arrangement runs two lines in parallel and agrees a shared checkpoint — for example, at the time set by the incident lead — before deciding on a rollback. The division follows who knows how, who is on shift and who has authority, not type.

The example illustrates how a team can consider customer impact alongside evidence that an action is justified. Real decisions about payments and rollbacks belong to the authorised team and follow its incident procedures.
### The review meeting: how to set the agenda

(Fictional scene.) At the next day's review there are two common agendas. One gives the on-call colleague a few minutes to describe the situation at the time, then walks the timeline item by item. The other aligns the timeline first to establish why the alert came ten minutes late, then comes back to people.

Both have costs. Talking only about the situation may miss the cause of the alert delay once more; walking only the timeline may leave the on-call colleague afraid to hit stop next time. Both have counterexamples: someone arguing to start with the situation will also put the timeline on the whiteboard and go through it, especially when blame has landed on the wrong person; someone arguing to start with the timeline will also ask "who was most tired last night" before getting to the point.

Order is not the criterion; the review is worth something when both happen. When setting the agenda, ask two questions: is what needs changing the process or the communication, and who most needs to be heard in this meeting. Different answers give different agendas, with no relation to type.

body: Treating "good at caring" as the property of Feeling types is the most common slip in this pair. Caring is a skill built through practice and experience; ESTP may be the first to notice a new colleague's hands shaking and pull them off the desk. Conversely, ESFJ under time pressure may push the schedule and lose track of who was left behind.

Treating "good with numbers" as a marker of Thinking types is equally wrong. ESFJ can work out how many orders a rollback would charge twice, and care more afterwards about how to explain it to customers; ESTP can do the same calculation and want to verify whether the criterion holds first.

The third slip is treating a rollback as a competence issue. "A release should be stable" is an expectation, not evidence about preference; willingness to roll back depends more on whether the criteria were written in advance, how clear the authority is, and whether observation has blind spots.

The fourth deserves its own line: using "called first or opened the dashboard first" as evidence of type. The same action may come from on-call division, change authority, an information gap, or an entirely different reason. Labelling on sight skips the reason, and the difference in this pair lies precisely in the reason.

One trade-off starts from the people: will this action make people who have already been charged pay twice, what can support say publicly right now, and how do we correct a statement issued too early. On the outward side, it more often wants to fix now who notifies whom and when to reassess, so the people waiting in the group have a definite answer. The cost is that the public line may be set before the facts, and the second statement becomes harder to write.

The other trade-off starts from measurable quantity: how many points the success rate has dropped, which data centre the failures concentrate in, and whether that criterion can be applied consistently across all channels. On the outward side, it more often prefers not to fix anything yet, closing once the next round of metrics arrives, so nothing has to be retracted immediately. The cost is that complaints may pile up while people wait, and support has nothing it can say.

Keep the counterexamples in both directions. Someone starting from the people will also demand that an entry point be closed at once, having calculated that it will not affect anyone mid-payment; someone starting from quantity will also ask support to send a short holding line because the channels are already pressing. Neither changes the direction of the preference; both show the two approaches are within range.

Sequence is not a criterion. Whoever has years of on-call experience, of either type, is more likely to walk the runbook once first; who holds the change authority that day and who is the shift lead often override preference. The same person may take the other approach on another shift.

### Why Fe and Ti are shared but sit in different places

The common four-function notation used here puts ESFJ at Fe–Si–Ne–Ti and ESTP at Se–Ti–Fe–Ni. Two names overlap: Fe and Ti. What changes is the perceiving side: Si and Ne against Se and Ni.

The two shared processes do not sit in the same place: Fe is dominant in ESFJ and third in ESTP; Ti is inferior in ESFJ and auxiliary in ESTP. A different position only means this writing places them in different slots; it does not explain when they appear, how practised they are, or who is better at anything.

The four preference letters each cover one thing. T/F covers what goes on the scales when choosing: a standard that can be applied consistently, or what the people involved have to carry. J/P covers the outward step: tightening the arrangement, or loosening it and waiting. The two cannot substitute for each other, and neither can be measured by how fast someone talks or how soft the tone is.

The third position is not the same process on both sides: Ne is third for ESFJ, Fe is third for ESTP, and Ni is fourth for ESTP. Whether that slot carries an attitude label is handled differently across tables; this page lists the common writing and does not present it as the only version. The disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain who speaks first. The preferences are set out one by one in the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [ESTP profile](/en/personality/estp).

Align the conditions first: the same release, the same dashboard, the same permissions, the same forty minutes. If one is the shift lead and the other was pulled in as support, the difference between the columns comes more from the division of work; if the runbook already fixes the trigger conditions, both columns move toward the runbook.

Either type can check the dashboard first, and either can notify support first. Each cell states which basis may be weighed more heavily in front of the same information, and which axis the row illustrates; none of it is a scale of ability or a behavioural prediction.

| Six moments in the same rollback call | ESFJ: the basis more likely weighed | ESTP: the basis more likely weighed | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Both consider the same response options after confirming the scope of the alert | Weigh how each option affects customers and what support they will need | Apply the same success and verification criteria to each option | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Both choose what to say in the same confirmed support update | Weigh which details would matter most to customers already waiting | Use the same rule for choosing relevant, confirmed details | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Someone proposes closing one entry point | Weigh how the same temporary closure would affect people in the middle of paying | Apply the same agreed impact and reversibility criteria that would be used for any comparable closure | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Halfway through, whether to settle the plan now | Agree on a provisional time and channel for the same update | Keep feasible times and channels open while the same metrics come in | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| Who notifies, and in what order | Agree on a provisional list of responsibilities for sending the same update | Keep several assignments open while availability is confirmed | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| How to sequence tomorrow's review | May agree on a provisional agenda covering the same review topics | May keep the agenda flexible while participants identify what needs discussing | Outward stance, leaning J/P |

sections.body_md:
Scope note: the scenes below are fictional and are used only to compare ways of communicating and organising information; they correspond to no real person or event. Whether and when to roll back follows your own service runbook and authority — this page provides no handling procedure; where money and customer data are involved, follow internal process and professional guidance first.

When the two work together, the usual sticking point is messages falling out of sync in the group: one is waiting for a number that can be stated publicly, the other is waiting for a scope that can be confirmed internally. It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of basis each needs first.

### Forty minutes after release: payment success rate falling

(Fictional scene.) Forty minutes after a new version ships, the payment success rate is below normal and complaints are coming in. Both hold the same dashboard, the same change ticket and the same permissions.

One handling pulls the affected list, groups it by channel, gives support different wording per channel, and sends the line "we are working on it" to steady the people already waiting. The possible cost is stating an estimated time too early, which makes the second statement harder to write.

The other checks whether failures are concentrated in one part of the service and asks whether the same evidence would justify a change elsewhere. Waiting for firmer evidence can delay an update to support. Either emphasis could inform the same decision, which belongs to the authorised team under its own runbook.

Either can rescue the situation and either can fail. A workable arrangement runs two lines in parallel and agrees a shared checkpoint — for example, at the time set by the incident lead — before deciding on a rollback. The division follows who knows how, who is on shift and who has authority, not type.

The example illustrates how a team can consider customer impact alongside evidence that an action is justified. Real decisions about payments and rollbacks belong to the authorised team and follow its incident procedures.

### The review meeting: how to set the agenda

(Fictional scene.) At the next day's review there are two common agendas. One gives the on-call colleague a few minutes to describe the situation at the time, then walks the timeline item by item. The other aligns the timeline first to establish why the alert came ten minutes late, then comes back to people.

Both have costs. Talking only about the situation may miss the cause of the alert delay once more; walking only the timeline may leave the on-call colleague afraid to hit stop next time. Both have counterexamples: someone arguing to start with the situation will also put the timeline on the whiteboard and go through it, especially when blame has landed on the wrong person; someone arguing to start with the timeline will also ask "who was most tired last night" before getting to the point.

Order is not the criterion; the review is worth something when both happen. When setting the agenda, ask two questions: is what needs changing the process or the communication, and who most needs to be heard in this meeting. Different answers give different agendas, with no relation to type.

sections.body_md:
Treating "good at caring" as the property of Feeling types is the most common slip in this pair. Caring is a skill built through practice and experience; ESTP may be the first to notice a new colleague's hands shaking and pull them off the desk. Conversely, ESFJ under time pressure may push the schedule and lose track of who was left behind.

Treating "good with numbers" as a marker of Thinking types is equally wrong. ESFJ can work out how many orders a rollback would charge twice, and care more afterwards about how to explain it to customers; ESTP can do the same calculation and want to verify whether the criterion holds first.

The third slip is treating a rollback as a competence issue. "A release should be stable" is an expectation, not evidence about preference; willingness to roll back depends more on whether the criteria were written in advance, how clear the authority is, and whether observation has blind spots.

The fourth deserves its own line: using "called first or opened the dashboard first" as evidence of type. The same action may come from on-call division, change authority, an information gap, or an entirely different reason. Labelling on sight skips the reason, and the difference in this pair lies precisely in the reason.
sections.title: ESFJ and ESTP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the item bank, version, language and scoring convention first, then which kind of experience you were referring to: your own choice when there was room, or what the process required you to do. Circumstances push answers to one side, and one score cannot establish a stable tendency.

Use two questions specific to this pair, without keeping score: when duties are clear and both options are viable, which standards do I use to weigh the cost of a wrong rollback against continued exposure? Facing an unconfirmed scope of impact, which arrangements do I want settled and which options kept, and why?

Record the reason along with the action, not the action alone. Behind the same action there may be "I am afraid customers will hear it from another channel" or "I am afraid this criterion will not apply to other channels", and the two point to different preferences. These notes are for reflection, are not scored, do not assign a type, and a few weeks of trend cannot replace an interpretation of the assessment result.
sections.title: ESFJ and ESTP: how to keep observing

items.answer:
They share E and S and differ on T/F and J/P: whether judgement more often rests on a standard applicable consistently or counts people and values in, and whether the outward step settles the arrangement or keeps options and waits.

In a rollback call, either may check the dashboard first, and either may brief support first. What discriminates better is which kind of basis is cited more often across comparable situations, and which end is treated as the premise. A single sequence or one phrasing cannot type anyone.
items.question: What is the core difference between ESFJ and ESTP?

items.answer:
They share Fe and Ti: Fe dominant in ESFJ and third in ESTP; Ti inferior in ESFJ and auxiliary in ESTP.

This page uses the common writing Fe–Si–Ne–Ti and Se–Ti–Fe–Ni; what changes is the perceiving side — Ne is third for ESFJ, while Fe is third and Ni fourth for ESTP. Whether the third position carries an attitude label varies across sources, so check whether a differing version states its source. Positions describe an ordering of emphasis only, and predict neither the order of behaviour, a field of expertise nor how well two people will work together.
items.question: Which two functions do they share, and where do the positions differ?

items.answer:
Both behaviours fit either type. T/F describes which criteria carry more weight, and J/P describes whether to settle an outward arrangement or keep options open.

Either person in the fictional incident could raise the customer impact or apply the same verification criteria across channels. The scope of the incident, responsibilities and available evidence help explain the order in which they act.
items.question: ESTP also reassures customers first, and ESFJ also acts at once — can they still be told apart?

items.answer:
Both can do it; who is more suitable is a competence judgement and cannot be derived from type.

Scheduling follows dashboard experience, change authority, outward communication and the shift division: on-call work is watching metrics, setting criteria, communicating outward and reviewing afterwards, and none of those four is allocated by type. When two people share a shift, run two workstreams in parallel and agree a cross-check time; neither should announce "recovered" alone.
items.question: Who is better suited to lead on-call for a release?

items.answer:
Most often on the statement and the incident falling out of step: a statement goes out while the incident continues, or the incident stops and nobody tells the customers.

A usable agreement ties the two to one point in time: every outward publication carries an internal review time, at which the other person confirms whether the metrics really turned. That agreement has nothing to do with type and applies to whoever is on shift; written into the runbook it is more reliable than remembered.
items.question: Where do ESFJ and ESTP most often get stuck on call together?

items.answer:
Check the item bank, version, language and scoring convention first, then which kind of experience you were referring to.

If the same tool reports interpretable preference scores, look at whether T/F and J/P sit near the boundary; sitting near it only means that item is sensitive to changes in your answers, not that two complete types both hold. Then recall which answers reflected your own choice and which reflected what the process required, without assuming which way the result should lean, and without assuming a retest in another setting would be more reliable.
